chapter_theme: The invocation to Shiva the dancer and the first eighteen poems of Palai Padiya Perunkadungo's paalaikkali: nearly every poem is a debate over leaving home for wealth, in which the friend or the wife sets love, youth and the household against the giving, conquest and gain that wealth promises, often with long argued refrains and moral similes drawn from kingship and impermanence; several end with the man turning back, and one (9) has ascetics defend an elopement as the way of virtue.

1.reading: The invocation asks Shiva, who spoke the Vedas to the brahmins, hid the Ganga in his matted hair, burned the three cities and goes eight-armed and dark-throated with fierce goblins behind him, whether, when he dances the kodukotti, the pandarangam and the kapalam, his consort does not keep for him the beat, the measure and the rhythm; and says that with her keeping them he danced for us.
1.nuance: The three dances are named in the order of the three musical terms the goddess supplies (சீர், தூக்கு, பாணி), and line 15 gathers the terms back in reverse; the god is made a dancer who needs a partner to keep time, a fitting opening for an anthology in the kali metre, which was sung. The last line (ஆணம் இல் பொருள் எமக்கு அமர்ந்தனை ஆடி) turns on the rare word ஆணம், and its sense is not settled.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god by his dances, the கடவுள் வாழ்த்து of paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the goddess, her waist slender as a creeper

2.reading: The friend tells the woman that when the man resolved to cross a waste split and burning as if Shiva had struck the three forts, she asked him three times whether wealth sought across hills because refusing a suppliant is shameful is truly wealth, unless it be not leaving the breast of the chaste wife who will not live without him, and that, told this is not love, he bowed like a tusker that no post can hold yet stops at the sound of the lute, and stayed by her word, afraid her old beauty would fade.
2.nuance: The friend grants the man the most honourable motive the Sangam knows, wealth to give to those who ask (இரந்தோர்க்கு ஒன்று ஈயாமை இழிவு), and still sets the wife's shoulders above it; the triple refrain changes only the word for what he crosses (மலை, கல், கடன்) and the word for her body. The tusker that breaks every tether but stops for the lute makes her speech the music that tames him.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's resolve to leave for wealth and its prevention

comparisons.tenor: Shiva's anger against the asuras, like a lion's
the sun's burning, like the face of the three-eyed god in anger
the hills split by the heat, like the forts falling when struck
the wife's chastity, worshipped like the northern star

comparisons.vehicle: கடும் களிற்று ஒருத்தல் யாழ் வரைத் தங்கியாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the man checked by the friend's words, as a wild tusker is held by lute music

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend reports to the wife how she dissuaded the man (lines 9 to 22 are her speech to him)

3.reading: The friend tells the man who is set on his venture that, since he would not heed their pleas that she, shamed by the gossip and wasting, will not live if he leaves, the things he will meet on the road (a dried spring with its flowers withered, a flowering creeper drooping from a withered tree, scorched young leaves) will themselves stop him, showing him, like kin who speak the truth, what has suffered as she has.
3.nuance: The friend gives up on persuasion and hands the argument to the landscape: each stanza pairs a plea refused with a withered thing that will stop him (தகைப்பன), so the paalai land, usually the danger, becomes her advocate. Because the poem states the likeness itself (இவள் போல்), the withered things are an open comparison, not a hidden one.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is about to leave her for his venture

comparisons.tenor: the spring, creeper and leaves on the road, which have suffered as she has
the forest that will check his going, like kin who tell the truth

4.reading: The friend tells the man that the woman knows he means to cross for wealth the waste where tiger-eyed bowmen kill travellers even with nothing to take, only to watch them writhe: she says that, not content with embracing her, he dresses her hair, not content with praising her mouth as sweeter than toddy, he sets her jewels straight, not content with gazing, he strokes her brow, and that this excess of tenderness hides something; she would not live a day without him, so let him give up this journey.
4.nuance: The woman reads the leaving in the caresses themselves: each refrain begins with what he does too much (அமையார், 'not content') and ends 'what is he thinking? I do not know'. The bowmen of the opening kill those who carry nothing, so the friend quietly answers the wealth motive in advance: on this road wealth protects no one.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's planned journey for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the bowmen's gaze, a tiger's
her budding teeth, sharp as thorns
the sweetness of her mouth, more delighting than toddy

5.reading: The friend tells the man that if he knew they were dearer to him than the wealth he would win across a waste where herds and elephants mingle with bowmen and paths are lost, he would not be like traders ruined when the wind seizes their ships; she asks whether the woman will bear it, desolate like a festival ground after the festival, like a land ravaged by its own rulers, or live like a lotus a night out of water, and says that on whatever day he goes her life will go.
5.nuance: Line 9 (நாளும் கோள்மீன் தகைத்தலும் தகைமே) is obscure; on one reading the friend says that holding back even the planets on their course would be fitting for such a man, an ironic concession. The close does not ask him to stay: it makes the date of his leaving the date of her death, so that he must choose a day knowing what it names.

thinai_evidence.note: the man weighing a journey across the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the man who leaves love for gain, like sea traders whose ships the wind took
her desolation, like a festival ground after the festival
her ruined face, like a land harried by those who rule it
her life without him, like a lotus a night out of water

6.reading: The woman answers the man who has painted the waste to her (antelope eating marral, the rains failed, travellers shot and shrunk, tongues dry for water, tears the only wetness) by asking why he speaks as if he did not know her: it is unlike him; if he would think of her with love and take her along with hardship for a companion, what other pleasure could she want?
6.nuance: She turns his deterrent catalogue round: the harder the road, the more it needs a companion; துன்பம் துணை ஆக makes hardship itself the shared thing. The plural எம் may be the friend speaking for her, as often in this book.

thinai_evidence.note: she asks to share the road he fears to take her on

comparisons.tenor: the man speaking as though he did not know her nature

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman (or the friend in her voice) answers his description of the road

7.reading: The friend asks the man, who means to cross a forest where a tusker worn by summer craves mirage water, one thing: as he plucks his bowstring her bright face darkens like the sun's disc clouded, as he binds his quiver and picks his arrows her eyes overflow like spring lilies meeting rain, as he strokes his chariot wheel her bangles slip like falling kodal petals; she suffers at the very noise of his going, so can the wealth he toils for in that land give her back her life?
7.nuance: The three stanzas pair each of his war-like preparations with a sign in her body (நீயே ... இவட்கே), so that the leaving happens twice, in his gear and in her; line 18 makes the point that she is undone by the noise of the preparations (அரவத்தும்) before he has gone.

thinai_evidence.note: the man preparing to leave for wealth across a summer forest

comparisons.tenor: her face growing pale, like the sun's disc darkened

comparisons.vehicle: சுனை மாண் நீலம் கார் எதிர்பவை போல்
comparisons.tenor: her eyes brimming with tears, like spring lilies taking the rain
her bangles slipping, like kodal petals falling

8.reading: The friend tells the man, who resolved without a word to cross a burnt hill-waste where the sun scorches like the sceptre of an unjust king and a weakened elephant leans on its tusks like a plough, that wealth is less stable than a lute whose seven strings fail when the middle one snaps, than Fortune who leaves those she embraced to be mocked, than a king who kills without mercy; he should not desire it and should stay, for to live in his own house under the king's protection, feeding guests, is wealth indeed.
8.nuance: Line 9 uses இறைச்சி in its plain sense, the delight the lute gives its lovers, not the poetic device. The poem ends by redefining wealth (அது மனும் பொருளே): the household that feeds guests under a just king is already what the journey seeks, which lets the friend oppose the journey on the householder's own terms.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's resolve to cross the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the sun's scorching, like the rule of a king who has chosen cruelty
the elephant's tusks dug into the ground, like a plough in dry earth
wealth, less lasting than a lute whose strings fail
wealth, less lasting than Fortune who deserts those she held
wealth, less to be trusted than a king who kills without pity

9.reading: A mother following her eloped daughter asks brahmin ascetics with umbrella, water-pot and triple staff whether they saw a girl and a boy joined in a love only they knew; they answer that they did, and, calling her the girl's mother, tell her that sandal is no use to the hill it grows on, pearls none to the sea, music none to the lute, but to those who wear and play them: so her daughter is to her; let her not grieve for a girl of surpassing chastity who has gone to follow the man she chose, for that is the way that never leaves virtue.
9.nuance: The answer comes from renouncers, the people least bound to household claims, and they judge the elopement by aram: following the chosen man is itself the righteous way (அறம் தலை பிரியா ஆறு). The three images all say that a thing's worth lies in its use by another, which cuts the parent's claim at the root.

thinai_evidence.note: a mother tracking a daughter who has eloped across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the daughter, who belongs to the man she goes with, not to the house she was born in
the daughter, of use to the one who wears her, not to the waters that bore her
the daughter, whose music is for the one who plays, not for the lute

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the brahmin ascetics on the road answer the mother, whose question (lines 1 to 8) is quoted; tradition gives the search to the foster mother, but the text says என் மகள்

10.reading: The friend tells the woman that she warned the man that the waste, its trees withered like a poor man's youth, shadeless like a mean man's wealth, burnt to the root like the end of one who harmed all and lost his name, dried like a world under a crooked-sceptred king whose men rob and kill, would break her who weeps if he only turns in bed, frets if he lingers in play, and grieves if his kind look fails; told that she would die if he went, the spear-bearing lord gave up the journey, so let her bangles sit tight again.
10.nuance: Each simile for the waste is a moral failure: the poor man's wasted youth, the mean man's wealth, the infamous man's end, the tyrant's realm. The paalai land is drawn from the ethics of the state and of giving, so the man who crosses it for wealth is shown the fate of wealth misused before he sets out.

thinai_evidence.note: a journey for wealth across the waste, now given up

comparisons.tenor: the withered branches, like a poor man's youth that bears no fruit
the shadeless trees, like a mean man's wealth that shelters no one
the trees burnt to the root, like the end of one who lost his name by harming all
the dried waste, like a land under a crooked-sceptred king whose agents seize and kill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend reports her plea to the man (lines 8 to 19) and his giving up the journey

11.reading: The woman tells her friend she is sure their lover, who left for wealth saying it brings the means to give to the deserving, victory over enemies and the joy of union, will return: when he said the forest was too hot to tread, leafless and burning, he also said that in it the tusker lets his mate drink the little muddy water before him, the dove fans its tired mate with its soft wings, and the stag gives its own shadow to the shadeless doe; such a forest will not make him wither her beauty, and the house lizard has chirped well and her eye throbs.
11.nuance: Three pairs carry the same iraicchi (the tusker that lets his mate drink first, the dove that fans its mate, the stag that shades the doe); the schema holds one carrier, so the elephant is tagged and the dove and stag are marked with the same role. Deleting any of them leaves her conclusion and the omens of lines 21 and 22 standing. Lines 1 to 3 name the three ends of wealth, giving, conquest and love, so the absence is justified by aram, porul and inbam at once; and she reads his own warnings about the forest against him.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman waits for the man who has gone for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the forest's heat, like fire

iraicchi.act: the tusker feeds his mate the little muddy water first and drinks after her
iraicchi.sense: the man who saw such care on his road will keep faith and come back to care for her

12.reading: The friend tells the man, who would leave her of the fragrant brow, who fears even if he sleeps a little apart, to cross a road where cairns over men killed by bowmen stand like a thorn fence and thirsty elephants lose their way among dried springs, that he calls the yield of his work true wealth, but youth and love will not stay in his hand; let him not let the days of embrace pass, for no one knows which day is the last, and he who spoils love for wealth goes the way of those who forget death and age.
12.nuance: The cairns (பதுக்கை) heaped over travellers killed on the road are memorials of violent death, not hero-stones, so they are scene here. The argument is a memento mori turned toward love: because the last day is unknown (கடை நாள் இது என்று அறிந்தாரும் இல்லை), the present embrace, not future wealth, is what must not be wasted.

thinai_evidence.note: the man about to leave her for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the line of cairns over the slain, like a long fence of thorn
the man who sets wealth above love, alike with those who forget death and age

13.reading: The friend tells the woman not to despair that he will leave: the man said that if she came with him across the burnt waste (black as a field a raging king has fired, where spotted does and stags run to mirages, monkeys droop and mortar-footed elephants suck mud) her lotus soles would blacken on the stones, she who sleeps on swan-soft beds would start at the cries of beasts, and her leaf-like body would wither in the wind off burning brush; unless the forest is truly hard he will not leave her; he said it in jest, to see her tremble.
13.nuance: The friend reinterprets the man's catalogue of dangers as a lover's teasing (நகை குறித்தனரே), so the same speech that elsewhere announces a parting is here a test of her fear. Line 16 (துலங்கு மான் மேல் ஊர்தி) is unclear: மான் may be the lion-carved bed or a mount.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's talk of a journey through the waste and of her coming with him

comparisons.tenor: the burnt land, like a field an angry king has camped on and fired
the doe's spots, like popped grain
the elephant's feet, like mortars
her soles, like lotus petals dipped in lac
her bed, soft as swan's down
her speech, like a parrot's
her body, tender as young leaves

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend reports the man's words (lines 10 to 21) and reads them as teasing

14.reading: The woman tells the man that she now knows that his old praise of her shoulders, eyes, teeth, brow, hair and breasts, sweetly spoken and then turned away, means estrangement; she asks whether, deluded, he has forgotten, and whether he has taken for truth strangers' talk that 'there is no wealth but wealth' and 'what can lovers do for those who have none', not knowing that wealth made by leaving the straight way is an enemy in this life and the next; let him count her as wealth too: to give up the craving for wealth gained by letting go their embrace is wealth indeed.
14.nuance: The poem quotes two proverbs of the wealth party (பொருள் அல்லால் பொருளும் உண்டோ; காதலார் எவன் செய்ப பொருள் இல்லாதார்க்கு) and assigns them to strangers (ஏதிலார்), then answers with the ethical claim that wealth got by leaving the straight way is hostile in both worlds. The last two lines pun on பொருள, wealth and true worth.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's turn from her toward the pursuit of wealth

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, soft as a pillow

comparisons.vehicle: நீலத்து ஏந்து எழில் மலர் உண் கண்
comparisons.tenor: her eyes, blue lilies
her white teeth, like jasmine buds
her dark hair, rain-cloud falling

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the inclusive நம்முள் நாம் (line 17) marks the woman as speaker; the friend may speak for her

15.reading: The friend asks the man, who would cross a road where bowmen with bowstrings that roar like lions and beards curled like a stag's horns, who do not flee even from kings' armies, wound men for gain without mercy, whether fresh wealth can restore her beauty, like young asoka leaves, once pallor eats it, whether learning and pure penance can restore her moon face once pallor covers it like the snake on the moon, whether lasting union can restore her lily eyes once they drip like a lamp spitting oil: wealth can be made any day, but will it bring back her youth once it has gone?
15.nuance: The three questions pit three goods the man might gain abroad, wealth, learning and penance, and lasting union, against three losses that none of them can restore. The close makes the asymmetry explicit: wealth recurs daily, youth does not, so the wealth journey is a bad exchange by the merchant's own reckoning.

thinai_evidence.note: the man setting out across the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the bowstring's twang, like a lion's roar
the bowmen's curled beards, like a stag's twisted horns
her beauty, like young asoka leaves
her face, like the cool-rayed moon
her face clouded by pallor, like the moon seized by the snake
her eyes, like fragrant blue lilies
her tears, like oil a lamp wick spits

16.reading: The friend tells the woman, whose eyes are pale and tearful and whose bangles slip, that she too has wished to beg the cloud to cool with rain the rocks on their lover's road, the sun to calm its rage, the wind-god to blow cool, and that it is useless to fret looking to gods for one who leaves for wealth; but virtue itself has run to block his venture, saying that the chaste woman who brings rain to the world in drought must not lose her colour to pallor.
16.nuance: The cloud, the sun and the wind are addressed as powers to be begged and praised, and the friend calls that hope vain; but she then invokes the one power she trusts, the chaste wife's own power over rain. The woman who cannot get the cloud to cool his road is herself the one who brings rain to the world, so virtue (அறன்) takes her part.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone across the burning waste for wealth

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend shares the woman's grief (நாம்) and then comforts her

17.reading: The friend tells the woman how she spoke to the man as he resolved to leave while she wasted: will her beauty, which wanes daily unlike the full moon, last until he returns? will life, cut short as death cuts a bud in a fragrant pool, last? will youth, fresh as a pool of opening flowers where bees feed new, last? and says that her words, like medicine a physician gives to a sound body, became a medicine that gladdened his heart, and the great hero gave up his going.
17.nuance: The moon simile is turned: the moon wanes and fills again, her beauty only wanes (நிலையாது). The physician's medicine given to a body already well suggests the man was never truly bent on going; her words only confirmed what his heart wanted.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's resolve to leave for work and its reversal

comparisons.vehicle: நீள் கதிர் அவிர் மதி நிறைவு போல் நிலையாது
comparisons.tenor: her beauty, which does not stay full as the moon does
life cut short, as death's turn comes to a bud
youth, like a pool of fresh flowers
her words to him, like medicine a physician gives to a healthy body

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: lines 5 to 16 are the friend's speech to the man, reported to the woman

18.reading: The woman tells the man not to plan to leave her, driven by desire for rare wealth: let him remember the designs he painted on her shoulders and the marks on his own chest; wealth does not lie waiting for those who go, and those who stay do not all starve; for those who have youth and love together, is wealth worth wanting? while their days last, even if they share one cloth, each holding the other with one hand, the life of the united is the only life, and youth once gone is hard to bring back.
18.nuance: The one-cloth couple (ஒன்றன் கூறு ஆடை உடுப்பவரே ஆயினும்) concedes poverty outright: the claim is not that they will be rich enough but that union outweighs want. Lines 5 and 6 answer the merchant's fear with plain observation, as if from experience.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is tempted to leave her for wealth

links.note: Both anthology invocations show Shiva by his marks with the goddess beside him: Akananuru 0 sets Umai at his side on the bull; Kalittokai 1 has her keep the beat, measure and rhythm while he dances.
links.teaches: Each love anthology gives the god a partner suited to its form: the Akananuru, a book of spoken poems, seats her beside him, while the sung Kalittokai makes her the one who keeps time for his dance, so the consort's role follows the anthology's metre.

links.note: Kalittokai 1 names three of Shiva's dances (kodukotti, pandarangam, kapalam); Tirumanthiram 2733 lists kodukotti and pandarangam among the dances whose king he is and places them in the nadis and at Tillai.
links.teaches: The dance names the Tirumanthiram files into a yogic doctrine were already in the oldest love anthology as stage dances with a partner keeping time, so the later mystic list inherited a performance repertoire, not a private vision.

links.note: Kalittokai 2 calls the wife's chastity bright as the northern star (வடமீன் போல்) and sets her shoulders above wealth for suppliants; Purananuru 122 says Kari gives his land to brahmins and his tribute to bards and keeps as his own only the shoulders of his wife chaste as the northern star (வடமீன் புரையுங் கற்பின்).
links.teaches: The puram poem shows the patron's answer to the dilemma the akam friend poses: a giver can give everything away and still keep the wife's shoulders as his only possession, so generosity and staying home need not be traded off as the man in Kalittokai 2 supposes.

links.note: In both the man leaves because he cannot refuse those who ask; in Akananuru 53 the wife says this means he loves wealth more than her and rejects the friend's calling it grace; in Kalittokai 2 the friend herself argues that such leaving is not love and wins.
links.teaches: The same honourable motive is judged in opposite directions by the same two persons in different poems: the friend excuses it in one and refutes it in the other, so the giving motive was a debated case in akam, not a settled virtue.

links.note: Kural 1152 says that union, which once gave delight even at a glance, now carries the pain of fearing separation; Kalittokai 4 shows the woman reading his coming departure in caresses that exceed the usual.
links.teaches: The poem supplies the mechanism the couplet leaves out: the fear spoils union because his tenderness itself has become the sign of leaving, so the more he gives the surer she is he will go.

links.note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kalittokai 5 ends: whatever day you go, on that day her life will go.
links.teaches: Both refuse the comfort of a promised return by tying her death to the moment of departure, and the Kalittokai shows the couplet's sharp line as the close of a full argument, after images of the emptied festival ground and the lotus out of water have prepared it.

links.note: In Kalittokai 13 the man lists what the waste would do to her if she came; in 6 the woman answers such a list by asking for hardship as her companion.
links.teaches: Read together, the danger catalogue is a convention both lovers know how to answer: in 13 the friend discounts it as teasing, in 6 the woman turns it into the reason to go together, so the list deters no one.

links.note: Kural 81 says the whole of living at home and guarding one's goods is for feeding guests; Kalittokai 8 ends that living in one's own house, protected by the king and tending guests, is itself wealth.
links.teaches: The friend turns the Kural's account of what wealth is for into an argument against the wealth journey: if a household already feeds its guests, it already has what wealth exists to buy.

links.note: Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so do at once what does; Kalittokai 8 says wealth is less stable than a lute, Fortune or a cruel king, so do not go after it.
links.teaches: From the same premise the two draw different conclusions: the Kural says to spend unstable wealth on lasting good, the love poem says not to leave love to seek it, so impermanence argued for staying home as well as for giving.

links.note: Both have a mother figure following an eloped girl and asking those on the road whether they saw her: in Akananuru 7 the foster mother asks a doe and a hill girl; in Kalittokai 9 the mother asks brahmin ascetics, who answer.
links.teaches: The Akananuru leaves the question unanswered on the empty road, while the Kalittokai brings in renouncers to answer it with a doctrine, so the later anthology turns the mother's lament into a debate the elopement wins.

links.note: In Akananuru 263 the mother says that had she known her daughter's mind she would have married her to the youth; in Kalittokai 9 the ascetics tell the mother that following the chosen man is the way of virtue.
links.teaches: What the Akananuru mother reaches only as regret, the Kalittokai states as a principle from outside the family: the girl's choice is rightful, so both books grant the eloping daughter the moral case against her parents.

links.note: Kural 557 likens the king's lack of grace to the world's lack of rain; Kalittokai 10 likens the drought-dried waste to a world under a crooked-sceptred king whose men rob and kill.
links.teaches: The comparison runs both ways: the ethics book explains tyranny by drought and the love poet explains drought by tyranny, so the bond between bad rule and failed rain was common enough to be used as vehicle or as tenor.

links.note: Both use an elephant who gives food to his mate on the road the man took; in Kalittokai 11 the woman concludes that such a forest will bring him back; in Akananuru 59 the friend sets the same care against the men who do not remember (உள்ளார்).
links.teaches: One image of animal care is made to argue both for and against the absent man's faithfulness, so the force of the iraicchi depends on the speaker's purpose, not on the creature.

links.note: In Kalittokai 11 the woman infers that the man who saw a stag shade its doe will come home; in Akananuru 34 the man, having seen a stag feed and guard its doe, urges his charioteer home.
links.teaches: The woman's inference is borne out from the man's side in the other anthology: the creature's care on the road does turn the traveller homeward, so the iraicchi is a shared convention both lovers trust.

links.note: Both say death comes unseen and no one knows the last day; the Naladiyar concludes that one must lay up provisions of virtue in time, Kalittokai 12 that one must not let the days of embrace pass for wealth.
links.teaches: The same reminder of death is used to opposite ends: the Jain moralist spends the uncertain time on merit, the love poet on love, so the memento mori did not belong to renunciation alone.

links.note: Kural 247 states that this world is not for those without wealth; Kalittokai 14 puts the like saying (காதலார் எவன் செய்ப பொருள் இல்லாதார்க்கு) in the mouths of strangers and rejects it.
links.teaches: A maxim the Kural states as fact is quoted in the love poem as hostile outsiders' talk, so the wealth maxim was public wisdom that akam speakers could set against love and refuse.

links.note: Kural 113 says to give up at once gain made by leaving fairness, even if it brings good; Kalittokai 14 says wealth made by leaving the straight way is an enemy in this life and the next.
links.teaches: The Kural allows that unfair gain may bring good and asks for sacrifice anyway, while the love poem denies it brings good in either world, so the woman's argument is stronger than the ethics book's rule.

links.note: Naladiyar 17 says youth falls like fruit, so do not desire a woman for her eyes; Kalittokai 15 says wealth can be made any day but youth cannot be brought back, so do not leave her.
links.teaches: From the same fact that youth passes, the moralist counsels turning from desire and the love poet counsels holding fast to it, so the two books read the brevity of youth as a reason for opposite lives.

links.note: Kural 55 says the wife who worships her husband commands rain; Kalittokai 16 calls the woman the chaste one who gives rain to the world in drought and says virtue will not let her pale.
links.teaches: The power the Kural states as a marvel works in the love poem as an argument: a woman who can bring rain cannot be left to waste, so the belief served to bind husbands as well as to praise wives.

links.note: In Akananuru 5 the man says he gave up the journey because of his wife's silent, tearful sign; in Kalittokai 17 the friend says her own words, like medicine, made him give it up.
links.teaches: The same outcome is credited to whoever speaks the poem, the husband to the wife's mute grief and the friend to her own argument, so the given-up journey is a shared ending each voice claims.

links.note: In Akananuru 51 the man tells his heart that wealth won by parting is not worth having and he will stay and hold her; in Kalittokai 18 the woman tells him the same and adds that even sharing one cloth, the united live the only true life.
links.teaches: The case against the wealth journey is made from both sides, and the woman's version goes further by accepting poverty outright, which the man's version never has to face.

source_issues: kalittokai: the core records carry no colophon thurai for any poem, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.
kalittokai:1: the invocation has no colophon thinai (the review notes some sources label it paalai); copied as null.
kalittokai:10 lines 5 and 21, kalittokai:16 line 9: ஃ restored from the old encoding (flag repaired).
kalittokai:16 line 14: a damaged word was replaced by the sangamtamil.com reading இடை (flag repaired); the sense (ஆர் இடை, the hard road) fits the refrain of lines 6 and 10.
kalittokai:5 line 9 (நாளும் கோள்மீன் தகைத்தலும் தகைமே) and kalittokai:1 line 17 (ஆணம்) are obscure; readings marked in nuance.
